title: National Facilitator for Sustainability and Transition Strategy Development
description:
About Asian Disaster Preparedness Center ADPC is a non-profit, autonomous regional organization, international in status, established for scientific, educational, developmental, and humanitarian purposes, with a vision of safer communities and sustainable development through disaster risk reduction. Established in 1986 as an outreach center of the Asian Institute of Technology (AIT), ADPC has evolved into an organization dedicated to building disaster and climate resilience across Asia and the Pacific. ADPC employs a wide range of professional expertise typically required for Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) and Climate Resilience (CR). ADPC develops and implements cross-sectoral projects/programs across the 15 Priority Areas of Action of its Strategic Action Plan 2026–2030: Risk Knowledge and Geoinformatics, Policy and Institutional System, Effective Localization for Resilience, Climate Services, Resilient Planning and Implementation, Preparedness and Anticipatory Action, Nature based Solutions, Financing for Resilience, Resilient Recovery, Food and Water Security, Disaster Risk Finance Insurance, Health Risk Management, Urban & Infrastructure Resilience, Private Sector Engagement, and ADPC Knowledge Academy. These Priority Areas of Action are complemented and underpinned by three cross-cutting enablers: gender equality and social inclusion, disaster and climate innovations, and regional and transboundary cooperation. Through its work, ADPC supports the implementation of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030, the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the New Urban Agenda, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the agenda defined at the World Humanitarian Summit in 2016, and other relevant international frameworks. For details, please refer to the ADPC website at http://www.adpc.net/ . Department Introduction: The Preparedness and Climate Action (PCA) Department of ADPC focuses on enhancing the preparedness, climate action, and adaptation capacities of governments, response organizations, volunteers, non-governmental organizations, the private sector, communities, and other traditional and non-traditional actors within the Disaster Risk Management and Climate Resilience Ecosystem. It emphasizes the importance of locally-led adaptation strategies as a critical component of effective climate action while striving to strengthen the capacity of institutions and at-risk communities to achieve faster, more efficient, and climate-resilient disaster recovery. The department collaborates with these actors to ensure that regional, national, sub-national, and local disaster preparedness, response, recovery, and climate action frameworks and implementation plans are developed and implemented well before disaster strikes, prioritizing climate resilience and integrating strategies to reduce risks and build resilience against future climate-related hazards. Statement of Intent The Preparedness and Climate Action (PCA) Department of the Asian Disaster Preparedness Center (ADPC), in partnership with the Ethiopian Disaster Risk Management Commission (EDRMC), is implementing the E nhancing M ulti-Hazard P reparedness for O ptimizing W arning and Early Response (EMPOWER) Program in Ethiopia, with technical and financial support from the Gates Foundation. The EMPOWER Program aims to strengthen the organizational, institutional and leadership capacities of Ethiopia's disaster risk management institutions at national and subnational levels. It is anchored in the Multi-Hazard, Impact-Based Early Warning and Early Action System (MH-IB-EW-EAS) Roadmap, developed by EDRMC and endorsed by the Government of Ethiopia. Building on previous institutional capacity-building initiatives, EMPOWER seeks to strengthen institutional systems, human resources, technical capacities and coordination mechanisms that can be sustained beyond the program period. As part of these efforts, a Sustainability and Transition Strategy will be developed through an EDRMC-led, consultative and evidence-informed process, with technical support and inputs from ADPC. The process will review institutional capacities, systems and functions developed through successive capacity-building investments, including EMPOWER, to identify what has been sustained, remaining gaps and lessons learned. It will examine priority functions and capacities required to support EDRMC's evolving mandate, appropriate institutional arrangements, resource requirements and feasible sustainability and transition pathways. The findings will also inform EDRMC's longer-term institutional development priorities and potential future programming, with stronger government ownership and sustainability considerations embedded from the outset. In this context, ADPC seeks to engage an experienced national facilitator to support the consultative process and development of the EMPOWER Sustainability and Transition Strategy during the period December 2026 to March 2027. Scope of Work The consultant will work closely with EDRMC leadership, relevant directorates and technical units, with overall coordination and technical support from the ADPC team, to facilitate an EDRMC-led process for developing the Sustainability and Transition Strategy. The consultant's role is to facilitate an objective, structured and participatory process, rather than to independently determine EDRMC's sustainability arrangements. The process will be guided by the principles of EDRMC leadership and ownership; function before financing; institutionalization rather than parallel arrangements; realism and feasibility; progressive transition; and future-oriented programming. 1. Conduct desk review and prepare the consultation framework Review the National Disaster Risk Management Policy (2024), the MH-IB-EW-EAS Roadmap, the EMPOWER program documents and progress reports, and relevant EDRMC policies, institutional strategies, organizational arrangements and capacity-development initiatives, including previous ADPC-supported programs, EMPOWER and other relevant partner-supported investments. Assess the institutional capacity-development journey, identifying key achievements, capacities and systems sustained over time, remaining gaps and lessons learned. Prepare a concise working paper outlining initial findings, institutional sustainability issues and strategic questions for consultation. Develop the consultation methodology, guiding questions and workplan in coordination with EDRMC and ADPC, and establish a common understanding with EDRMC leadership on the purpose, scope and expected results of the exercise. 2. Facilitate Institutional Consultations, Sustainability Assessment and Strategic Planning Facilitate consultations with EDRMC leadership, directorates and technical units to identify priority institutional functions, capacities and systems required to fulfil EDRMC's evolving mandate under the National DRM Policy (2024), including functional linkages with sector ministries and sub-national DRM structures. Assess institutional ownership, existing capacities, human resources and surge-capacity arrangements, operational and ICT systems and their recurrent costs (e.g., software licences, hardware, situation room and data-server infrastructure), resource requirements, partnerships and sustainability challenges, taking into account previous investments in institutional capacity building. Examine feasible institutionalization and sustainability arrangements, including integration into government structures, capacity transfer, recurrent financing and continued technical or partner support. Develop a sustainability and institutionalization mapping, presenting options for discussion rather than predetermined commitments, that captures priority functions, institutional responsibilities, resource requirements, sustainability options and lessons learned from previous capacity-building investments. Facilitate strategic consultations with EDRMC, ADPC and, as appropriate, the Gates Foundation to review assessment findings and identify feasible sustainability and transition pathways. Support discussions on institutional priorities, ownership, financing options, partnerships and progressive transition of technical support, with a focus on strengthening EDRMC's long-term institutional capacity for disaster risk reduction, resilience building and self-reliance, including its ability to coordinate, operate, maintain and improve the MH-IB-EW-EAS using its own structures, people, procedures and resources after EMPOWER ends. Identify institutional or policy matters requiring higher-level government decisions and propose appropriate engagement approaches to secure necessary institutional commitments and resources. Document agreed directions, outstanding issues and strategic considerations for potential future capacity-development programming. 3. Develop and finalize the Sustainability and Transition Strategy Prepare a draft EDRMC-led Sustainability and Transition Strategy and Action Plan, drawing on consultation findings, institutional priorities and agreed strategic directions. Develop a practical, phased action plan identifying priority actions, institutional responsibilities, indicative timelines, resource considerations and sustainability indicators, including actions that can begin during the remaining EMPOWER implementation period. Facilitate review of the draft and a validation discussion with EDRMC, ADPC and the Gates Foundation, as appropriate, to confirm the proposed sustainability pathways, institutional responsibilities and priority actions. Incorporate feedback and submit the final Strategy and Action Plan by 10 March 2027 . Expected Deliverables This is an output-based consultancy. Payment will be made upon acceptance of each deliverable by ADPC, in consultation with EDRMC, as follows: Deliverable 1 – [20]%; Deliverable 2 – [40]%; Deliverable 3 – [40]%. The consultant is expected to deliver the following: Inception Report and Consultation Framework: Outlining the methodology, workplan, initial mapping of programs’ supported functions, the working paper on emerging sustainability issues and strategic questions for consultation, preliminary review of EDRMC's institutional capacity-development journey, lessons from previous capacity-building investments, and proposed consultation approach. Institutional Sustainability Assessment and Consultation Report: Consolidating findings from institutional and strategic consultations, including priority functions, existing capacities, institutional responsibilities, sustainability challenges, resource and financing requirements, and feasible institutionalization and transition options. The report will include the sustainability and institutionalization matrix and document key stakeholder discussions, agreed directions, outstanding issues and priority actions. Sustainability and Transition Strategy and Action Plan: Developed in consultation with EDRMC and reflecting assessment findings and agreed sustainability priorities. The strategy will outline institutional responsibilities, phased actions, resource requirements, milestones, and indicators to strengthen long-term institutional capacity, disaster risk reduction, resilience building and self-reliance. It will include a priority action plan for the remaining EMPOWER implementation period and strategic considerations for potential future programming in Ethiopia. The final version will incorporate feedback from EDRMC, ADPC and the Gates Foundation, as appropriate. Deliverable 1: Inception Report & Consultation Framework Timeline: Dec 2026 Deliverable 2: Institutional Sustainability Assessment and Consultation Report Timeline: Jan-Feb 2027 Deliverable 3: Sustainability Strategy Timeline: Feb - Mar 2027 Working Principles: In performing the duties and responsibilities above, the consultant will be supervised by the ADPC Program Manager based in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and work in close coordination with a designated EDRMC focal point, who will facilitate access to relevant directorates, personnel and information. ADPC will provide relevant documentations and evidence and will support the organization of consultation and validation meetings. All deliverables will be reviewed by EDRMC and ADPC prior to acceptance. Required Qualifications and Experience The consultant should demonstrate the following: Postgraduate degree in Disaster Risk Management, Public Policy, Public Administration, Institutional Development, Development Studies, or a related field. At least 7 years of relevant professional experience in institutional capacity development, organizational strengthening, strategic planning, or sustainability and transition planning, preferably within government or public-sector institutions. Proven experience in facilitating institutional assessments, strategic consultations, and multi-stakeholder planning processes, particularly with government leadership and technical departments. Demonstrated experience in developing institutional sustainability strategies, transition plans, capacity development frameworks, or related strategic and operational plans, including practical implementation arrangements. Good understanding of disaster risk management, multi-hazard early warning systems, and institutional arrangements for disaster preparedness and response. Experience assessing institutional functions, human resource capacities, operational systems, financing requirements, and options for sustaining externally supported investments. Familiarity with government institutional structures, planning and budgeting processes, and coordination mechanisms in Ethiopia; prior experience with EDRMC or the national DRM system is an advantage. Strong analytical, stakeholder engagement, facilitation, and report-writing skills, with the ability to translate consultation findings into actionable recommendations, responsibilities, milestones, and resource considerations. Experience working with government institutions, development partners, and international organizations is highly desirable. Excellent proficiency in English and Amharic is required. Duty Station: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia Duration: December 2026 – March 2027 The consultancy is expected to require 30 working days, spread over a three and a half month period from December 2026 to March 2027. A detailed work schedule, including consultations and deliverable deadlines, will be mutually agreed upon at the commencement of the assignment, in coordination with EDRMC and ADPC. Indicatively, the level of effort is [8] days for Deliverable 1, [12] days for Deliverable 2 and [10] days for Deliverable 3. The final Strategy is due by March 2027; the remaining period allows for any final review and contract close-out. Itinerary: During official missions outside the duty station, the Consultant will be entitled to local/international travel, daily subsistence allowance, accommodation, and other related travel costs as per ADPC financial policy. All travel must be pre-approved by ADPC and undertaken only upon written request and consent by the ADPC.

How to Apply: Interested candidates can submit the Technical and [Financial proposal ](https://docs.google.com/document/d/13UWXC5VTV9zMlHPKFziM28BU4QkO2wmB/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=101136916941119310787&rtpof=true&sd=true)with the completed [ADPC application form](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1n0dBsHfThGITa_CfLEHqvVnj5Ptvv-1v/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=101136916941119310787&rtpof=true&sd=true) (downloadable from www.adpc.net), resume, copy of degrees/certificate(s) together with a cover letter, to: [Google Link](https://forms.gle/J7CbbCNUVCbZrwJR8) or [https://forms.gle/J7CbbCNUVCbZrwJR8](https://forms.gle/J7CbbCNUVCbZrwJR8) by midnight Bangkok time on **30 November 2026.** Applications will be evaluated on technical merit (\[70\]%) and the financial proposal (\[30\]%); only shortlisted candidates will be contacted. **Female candidates are especially encouraged to apply.** ADPC encourages diversity in its workplace and supports an inclusive work environment.

title: Regional Humanitarian Manager - Horn, Eastern, Central and Southern Africa
description:
Cordaid is an international organisation for development and humanitarian assistance, working especially in fragile and conflict-affected regions. Guided by Christian values of human dignity, justice and compassion, we work towards a world without poverty and with equitable opportunities for all. More than 1.9 billion people live in fragile contexts where access to essential services and opportunities is limited. Together with our partners, we support locally led programmes in longer term development that strengthen healthcare, education, agrifood and justice systems. When crises occur, we work alongside local organisations to provide humanitarian assistance. Cordaid has regional offices in Europe, West-Africa, Horn, East, Central and South Africa and in the Middle East and Asia. Cordaid operates through a domain-based model. Our regional and country teams work with local partners so they can lead humanitarian response. Cordaid provides the local actors with capacity, technical advice and helps them meet humanitarian standards, engage with donors and fulfil their commitments. Cordaid is looking for a Regional Humanitarian Manager - Horn, Eastern, Central and Southern Africa (HECSA) (Fulltime, home-based in the HECSA region) As our Regional Humanitarian Manager for HECSA, you provide strategic leadership for humanitarian action, emergency preparedness, and crisis response across the region. Working at the interface between the HECSA Regional Core and the global Humanitarian Assistance Platform, you ensure that humanitarian responses are principled, locally led, and effectively integrated into regional strategies and Country Engagement Models (triple nexus approach). You serve as the organization's primary regional humanitarian focal point, representing HECSA in regional humanitarian coordination, policy, and advocacy spaces, and building strategic relationships with key stakeholders, first and above our networks of Caritas and ACT Alliance and also including UN agencies, donors, INGOs, regional bodies, and local humanitarian actors. Rather than managing direct programme implementation, you enable local partners to lead by strengthening preparedness, technical quality, and organisational readiness. You report directly to the HECSA Regional Director and to the global humanitarian manager. What you do Humanitarian Leadership & Strategy : Provide strategic leadership and advice on humanitarian action across the HECSA region, supporting Regional Directors and Country Engagement Models in rapid crisis decision-making Emergency Preparedness & Response : Strengthen regional preparedness and crisis readiness by coordinating regional contingency planning and supporting emergency response activations, Humanitarian Partnerships & Localisation : Foster equitable partnerships with national and local humanitarian partners across HECSA, with a partner led approach. Triple Nexus & Sectoral Integration : Spearhead the humanitarian-development-peace nexus approach across the region, linking emergency response and recovery to longer-term resilience, climate adaptation, and systems strengthening. Technical quality and accountability : Work with Cordaid’s global humanitarian team to uphold humanitarian principles, apply the Core Humanitarian Standard and the Sphere Standards, integrate protection across programmes, and ensure that crisis-affected people can give feedback and receive a response. Resource Mobilization & Positioning : Support engagement with major institutional humanitarian donors (ECHO, BHA, Dutch Relief Alliance, UN agencies) and work closely with the Business Development Manager to build a healthy regional humanitarian funding pipeline. Networking, Representation & Advocacy : Represent the Regional Core in regional humanitarian coordination clusters, UN/OCHA meetings, ACT Alliance and Caritas (country) fora, INGO platforms, and donor forums to advance strategic priorities and advocate for locally led responses. Risk Management, Safeguarding & Integrity : Implement Cordaid’s Integrity Compliance Framework, manage operational and contextual risks in fragile environments, and champion high standards of duty of care and safety. Who you are You hold a Master’s degree in Humanitarian Assistance, International Development, Disaster Management, International Relations, or a related field. Minimum of 10 years of progressively responsible experience in humanitarian leadership, emergency response, and crisis management in complex, fragile, and conflict-affected environments. Evidence of leading emergency responses in fragile settings, working with local partners that lead delivery, and representing an organisation with donors and humanitarian coordination bodies. Deep knowledge of the humanitarian sector and complex crisis dynamics across Horn, Eastern, Central or Southern Africa (HECSA). Sound practical expertise in Core Humanitarian Standards (CHS), SPHERE guidelines, cash transfer modalities, protection mainstreaming, and the triple nexus approach. Proven track record in working through national/local partners, driving localisation, and supporting partner capacity sharing in emergency settings. Demonstrated experience engaging with institutional humanitarian donors (ECHO, BHA, DRA, UN/CBHF) and multi-stakeholder humanitarian networks. Strong strategic thinking, decision-making, analytical, and financial management skills. Exceptional oral and written communication skills in English. Proficiency in French, Portuguese, Arabic, or relevant regional languages is a distinct advantage. Willingness to be home-based in the HECSA region with flexibility to travel up to 50% of the time within the region. You recognize yourself in Cordaid’s mission and values. What we offer A high-profile senior leadership position within an international, professional organization with a focus on social impact. A varied, highly impactful, and autonomous role where strategic initiative and vision are essential. A global organization with a strong commitment to social entrepreneurship and locally led impact. Good international working conditions and excellent secondary benefits. An initial contract for 1 year with the intention of extending, home-based within the HECSA region.

How to Apply: **How to apply** Applications including a motivation letter and CV in English for the attention of Human Resources, including the contact details of references at the last two employers can be uploaded through our website. Your application must be received by **30 November 2026** at the latest. Cordaid is fully committed to a safe working environment and the highest integrity standards. To read more on our commitment to Integrity, click here: [https://www.cordaid.org/en/who-we-are/integrity-and-code-of-conduct/](https://www.cordaid.org/en/who-we-are/integrity-and-code-of-conduct/). An integrity screening will be part of this application procedure. Cordaid signed up to the IASC Misconduct Disclosure Scheme. An assessment and / or a presentation of a “case study” can be part of the selection procedure. For more information about Cordaid, please visit our website: [www.cordaid.org](http://www.cordaid.org/) *Acquisition regarding this vacancy is not appreciated.*

title: Terms of References (ToR) for a Consultancy to Conduct a Feasibility Study for the proposed project: A Voice for Inclusion.
description:
Terms of References (ToR) for a Consultancy to Conduct a Feasibility Study for the proposed project: A Voice for Inclusion – Equal Education and a Strong Civil Society for Children with Disabilities in Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia. Assignment period: December 2026 – January 2027 Location:Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia Commissioned by:ChildFund Main Partners: ChildFund Deutschland, ChildFund Ethiopia, ChildFund The Gambia, ChildFund Zambia, Tesfa Birhan, Saama Kairo Federation, Chibombo/Mumbwa Child Development Agency, Kafue Child Development Agency Donor: Project to be submitted to BMZ Background and Context Context of the assignment Despite the ratification of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) by Ethiopia (in 2010), The Gambia (in 2015) and Zambia (in 2010), many children with disabilities continue to face significant barriers to accessing and successfully completing primary education. Children with severe or multiple disabilities, intellectual or learning disabilities, sensory impairments, and disabilities that remain unidentified are often among the most excluded. Exclusion is further compounded by factors such as gender, age, poverty and geographical remoteness. In addition, the absence of systematic processes for identifying children with disabilities frequently limits their access to appropriate support services, accommodations and referral mechanisms. Preliminary problem analyses conducted in all three countries suggest a number of common barriers and root causes. At family and community level, these include poverty and disability-related costs, transport and distance barriers, limited awareness of available support services, stigma and discrimination, weak parent support structures, safety concerns, and low expectations regarding the educational potential of children with disabilities. At school level, challenges include inadequate teacher preparation for inclusive education, insufficient follow-up coaching and mentoring, limited availability of assistive devices and adapted learning materials, inaccessible infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms, and constrained institutional and financial resources. Across all three countries, gaps are also evident between national policy commitments and their implementation at district, community and school levels. Common issues include weak coordination between sectors and administrative levels, insufficient funding, limited use of disability-disaggregated data, weak referral systems, and limited opportunities for meaningful participation of children with disabilities and their caregivers in planning and decision-making processes. In Zambia, UNCRPD commitments are domesticated through the Persons with Disabilities Act No. 6 of 2012, which provides for the right to inclusive education and established the Zambia Agency for Persons with Disabilities (ZAPD), alongside the Education Act of 2011 and the Children’s Code Act of 2022. The free education policy introduced in 2022 removed school fees, yet children with disabilities in rural and peri-urban districts such as Kafue, Mumbwa and Chibombo continue to face barriers that fee removal alone does not address, including distance to school, limited district-level assessment and specialised services, few teachers trained in inclusive or special education, and stigma. In The Gambia, commitments under the UNCRPD are supported by the Disability Act (2021), the Children’s Act, and the Ministry of Basic and Secondary Education’s Inclusive Education Policy Framework. Despite these policy commitments, children with disabilities continue to face significant barriers to accessing quality education, including late identification of disabilities, limited availability of specialised assessment and support services, inadequate assistive and learning resources, social stigma, and insufficient capacity within mainstream schools to respond to diverse learning needs. These challenges are often more pronounced in rural and underserved communities. In Ethiopia, commitments to inclusive education are operationalised through the Constitution (Article 41), the education policy framework, and the current Special Needs/Inclusive Education Strategy (2022/23-2029/30), which aims to ensure equitable access to quality education for children, youth and adults with special educational needs and disabilities. Despite this strong policy commitment, significant barriers continue to hinder implementation at federal, regional, woreda and school levels, including weak disability data systems, limited early identification and referral mechanisms, shortages of trained inclusive education professionals, inadequate assistive devices and adapted learning materials, inaccessible infrastructure, and persistent stigma. These challenges are often compounded by poverty, displacement, geographical isolation and gender-related disadvantages, particularly in rural, pastoralist, conflict-affected and underserved communities. While the analyses point to significant similarities in the patterns of exclusion across Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia, they are also highlighting important contextual differences. This creates opportunities for structured cross-country learning, knowledge exchange and the adaptation of effective approaches across different contexts. The planned project aims to address these challenges with an integrated micro-meso-macro approach: communities and families are sensitized and empowered; schools are developed into inclusive learning environments, mainly through training and development plans; and civil society organisations are strengthened to carry out advocacy work for inclusive education. The multi-country nature of the program offers an opportunity to generate evidence, promote cross-learning and identify scalable approaches that can strengthen inclusive education systems beyond the targeted locations. Inclusive education is both a rights-based obligation and a strategic investment in human capital, social inclusion and sustainable development. Ensuring that children with disabilities can access and succeed in education contributes to national development priorities, advances SDG 4 commitments, and supports broader efforts to ensure that no child is left behind. Brief about ChildFund International as the organization commissioning the study ChildFund International is a global child- and youth-focused development and humanitarian organization dedicated to advancing the well-being, resilience, and rights of children and young people, particularly those facing vulnerability and exclusion. Working through local partners, communities, governments, and civil society, ChildFund promotes locally led and owned development approaches that strengthen systems, build community capacity, and create sustainable impact for children and their families. Its programmes focus on education, child protection, health, livelihoods, and youth empowerment, with an emphasis on achieving lasting outcomes that enable children and young people to learn, thrive, and contribute meaningfully to their communities. This assignment is commissioned by ChildFund International to inform the design and implementation of a multi-country inclusive education programme in Ethiopia, The Gambia, and Zambia. The International Office (IO) will provide overall strategic direction, technical leadership, and quality assurance; the Africa Regional Office (RO) will provide regional coordination, technical oversight, and facilitate cross-country learning; while the respective Country Offices (COs) will lead country-level coordination, stakeholder engagement, and contextual guidance to ensure the study reflects national priorities and local realities. Brief about the proposed project The proposed multi-country programme seeks to improve equitable access to, participation in, and quality of inclusive primary education for children with disabilities in Ethiopia, The Gambia, and Zambia. The programme is founded on the recognition that educational exclusion results from interconnected barriers at household, community, school, and systems levels, requiring a coordinated and multi-level response. Through a locally grounded and systems-strengthening approach, the programme aims to ensure that children with disabilities, including those who are currently out of school, are identified, enrolled, actively engaged in learning, and able to make measurable progress in foundational literacy and numeracy. Particular attention will be given to children facing multiple and intersecting forms of exclusion, including girls with disabilities, children with high support needs, children living in poverty, and those in remote or underserved areas. To achieve these outcomes, the programme will pursue an integrated micro-meso-macro approach that combines community engagement, inclusive school development, institutional capacity strengthening, and policy engagement through four complementary result areas. Proposed Output 1: Family and Community Environment Children with disabilities will be identified through community-based identification and referral mechanisms. Parents/caregivers will be supported to promote school enrolment and effectively address the learning needs of children with disabilities, including through effective referral systems and linkages to service providers, in line with the programme's systems-strengthening and sustainability objectives. Parents/caregiver self-help groups will be established and/or strengthened to address barriers to education and support sustained participation, retention, and educational success for children with disabilities. Proposed Output 2: Inclusive Schools and Learning Environments Target schools will be supported to strengthen inclusive teaching and learning practices through teacher training, coaching and mentoring and the development of learning materials and methods aligned with the needs of children with disabilities. Existing school structures will be trained and supported to introduce inclusive school development plans, thereby embedding inclusive practices within school systems and leadership structures to support long-term implementation, ownership, and scalability beyond the life of the programme. Model schools will be equipped with accessible infrastructure, demonstrating how accessible learning environments contribute to sustainable institutional change and improved learning outcomes; while other project schools will be supported to identify, prioritise and cost accessibility improvements, with project funding complementing local resources and budgets where available. Proposed Output 3: Civil Society Capacity and Advocacy Through cross-national learning and collaboration, civil society organisations will strengthen their capacity to generate and use evidence on effective and cost-efficient inclusive education practices, engage in evidence-based advocacy, and promote the active participation of persons with disabilities and their representatives in education policy processes. A joint cross-national platform will facilitate the long-term exchange of evidence, implementation experiences, costing data and advocacy tools to support the institutionalisation and financing of inclusive education practices. Proposed Output 4: Policy Implementation and Local Adoption Under Output 4, civil society organisations and OPDs will be supported to translate evidence and lessons learned from project implementation and cross-country exchange into advocacy messages, policy recommendations and budget proposals for inclusive education. Through engagement with policy-makers, planning bodies and coordination mechanisms, opportunities will be created to foster government ownership and to promote the uptake of effective and cost-efficient inclusive education practices within planning, budgeting and resource allocation processes. This will support the use of evidence to inform scalable and sustainable system-level improvements, strengthen the institutionalisation of inclusive education practices within government systems, and contribute to the sustained delivery of inclusive education services beyond the project period. Through these interconnected interventions, the programme aims to contribute to a situation in which children with disabilities in the target communities are able to enrol in school, participate effectively in classroom learning and achieve measurable improvements in foundational literacy and numeracy. In the longer term, the programme seeks to strengthen inclusive education systems and support the sustainable implementation of inclusive education policies and practices across the three participating countries. Purpose and Scope of the Feasibility Study Study Type A feasibility study provides an evidence-based foundation for project design and investment decisions by assessing implementation readiness, opportunities, risks, and key assumptions and offering guidance and possible improvements. The findings will inform programme optimisation and effectiveness, identify pathways for sustainable and scalable impact, and help ensure that resources are directed towards interventions with the greatest potential to improve inclusive education outcomes. Purpose of the Study The purpose of the feasibility study is particularly to assess the feasibility of the proposed project and systematically examine the extent to which the project approach can plausibly achieve the planned changes under the existing conditions. Specifically, the study focuses on these specific topics: 1. Evidence Base and Context Analysis Identify and review relevant international, regional and national evidence related to disability-inclusive primary education, including successful approaches, lessons learned, policy frameworks, implementation models and emerging good practices. Establish baseline information on the current situation of children with disabilities, schools, communities and relevant stakeholders in the target areas in order to inform project design and future monitoring. All proposed baseline data should be disaggregated by region/district, sex, age, grade/educational level and type of disability. Map existing systems, services, structures and coordination mechanisms relevant to disability-inclusive education and determine where the project should strengthen existing systems, fill critical gaps or avoid duplication of existing initiatives. 2. Relevance and Strategic Fit Evaluate the relevance of the proposed project activities, objectives and strategies in relation to the needs of target groups, existing systems and the broader context. Assess the strategic rationale and expected added value of the proposed multi-country approach compared to separate country-level interventions. The study should analyse common challenges, complementary strengths, opportunities for cross-country learning, joint advocacy, knowledge exchange, mutual capacity development and the transfer of effective inclusive education practices, as well as factors that justify the selection of Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia as participating countries. Recommend practical and financially realistic strategies for ensuring that the project benefits children with different types of disabilities, including those who are often most excluded, such as children with intellectual disabilities, communication difficulties, multiple disabilities and higher support needs. 3. Validation of the Proposed Intervention Validate the project's Theory of Change, he proposed indicators, baseline and target values and recommend revisions where necessary to ensure realistic and measurable results; also assess the plausibility of the proposed causal pathways and expected outcomes. Assess how the proposed intervention can most effectively contribute to meaningful participation and measurable improvements in foundational literacy and numeracy outcomes for children with disabilities. The study should identify critical success factors, potential barriers and additional measures required to ensure that increased enrolment and attendance translate into improved learning outcomes. Assess the availability and capacity of existing systems for feasible, ethically appropriate, disability-responsive assessment, identification, referral and learning support/educational-support pathways, referral completion, feedback loops, case follow-up and service-capacity constraints. This should include an analysis of whether learning assessments can be adapted to different impairments, the uptake of Universal Design for Learning in the target schools so far, the availability of specialised teaching and learning materials and assistive devices, and the capacity of government services, OPDs and other actors to assess children's needs and facilitate access to appropriate support. Test key assumptions underlying the project design, including assumptions related to identification and referral systems, teacher retention, stakeholder engagement, service availability, maintenance of infrastructure, the added value of cross-country learning and the sustainability of project-supported approaches. Assess the feasibility of local adoption and financing of tested inclusive education practices by schools, local authorities and government structures, including opportunities for incorporation into existing planning, budgeting, supervision and school improvement systems Assess the integration of cross-cutting issues, including gender equality, child safeguarding, conflict sensitivity and environmental sustainability. 4. Capacity and Feasibility Assessment Assess the operational feasibility of the proposed intervention, including availability of resources, institutional arrangements and stakeholder commitment at community, district and national levels. Assess the organisational and technical capacities of the proposed implementing partners and evaluate whether the proposed intervention is realistic and proportionate to their current capacities. The study should identify existing strengths, capacity gaps and the capacity development measures required to enable partners to successfully implement, monitor and sustain the proposed interventions. Identify external factors, contextual influences and implementation risks that may affect the achievement and sustainability of project results. Assess the likelihood that project-supported approaches, services and practices can be sustained, institutionalised and financed by local actors after project completion. 5. Optimisation and Recommendations Assess the extent to which the proposed project design is realistic within the available budget and identify opportunities for simplification, prioritisation and cost-efficiency. Review and, where necessary, refine the proposed intervention strategy, impact matrix, outputs and indicators (including baseline and target values) based on study findings, including the development of recommendations for indicators and targets that have not yet been defined. Provide evidence-based recommendations for improving project design, implementation arrangements, targeting, monitoring, partnership development, capacity strengthening, sustainability and scalability Assessment Criteria The study should present the context of the planned project at all relevant levels (micro, meso, macro) and also include key data relevant to the project regarding the initial situation. Building on this, an analysis should be carried out to determine the extent to which the chosen approach can contribute to resolving the problem for the target groups and other stakeholders. Recommendations for adjustments to the specific project concept – including the draft impact matrix and suggested measures – should be formulated in as concrete a manner as possible. In doing so, consideration must be given to the actors and stakeholders to be involved, proposals for areas to be monitored in terms of outcome and impact measurement, and the opportunities and risks involved. Furthermore, the proposed project should be critically assessed in the light of the OECD DAC criteria of relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact and sustainability: Relevance: Does the planned project approach address a key development issue or a critical development bottleneck in the partner countries? Are the focus, priorities and objectives (approach) of the planned project aligned with the target groups and clearly defined? To what extent do the intervention objectives and design adequately take into account the specific needs of the target groups and structural barriers in the project countries, the partner organisations, and the political programmes? Are the norms and standards of the approach compatible with those of the target groups? Is the project designed with conflict sensitivity in mind (the ‘Do No Harm’ principle)? Coherence: To what extent are the planned activities consistent with human rights principles (inclusion, participation), conventions and relevant standards/guidelines? To what extent are there synergies and links between the planned project and other interventions by the same partners and other actors? What overlaps or common ground exist between the target groups of this project and those of other actors’ projects in the same context? To what extent does the intervention add value and avoid duplication of effort? Effectiveness: Are the causal relationships (including assumptions) plausible? What negative effects might arise? Is the chosen methodological approach appropriate to the context and sufficient to achieve the project’s objective? At what level (multi-level approach) should additional measures be planned to increase effectiveness? How will changes be measured (baseline and endline tools)? Are the indicators in the draft impact matrix suited for this? Efficiency: To what extent can the planned measures be implemented within the planned timeframe and allocated funds? Which staffing investments, operating costs and staffing levels are recommended proportionate to the intended objectives? Impact: How does the project objective (outcome) contribute specifically to the overarching objective (impact)? To what extent does the planned project contribute to structural development, serve as a model and have a broad, cross-national impact beyond progress within each country and beyond the project period? At what levels are standards or structures being changed? Sustainability: How can the sustainability of the results and impacts be ensured and strengthened (structurally, economically, socially, environmentally)? What long-term capacities are being built up within the target group to enable them to continue the implemented measures independently? What positive changes (role behaviour, mechanisms, networks and others) benefit civil society in the long term? What personnel risks for those implementing the measures, as well as institutional and contextual risks, affect sustainability, and how can these be minimised? On the basis of the key findings relating to the purpose of the study and the assessment of the project concept against the DAC criteria, the study should make clear recommendations which specific proposals and improvements should be incorporated into the project concept. Key assessment questions Building on the specific topics described above and the OECD-DAC criteria described, the study should address the following key questions: 1. Purpose and use of the feasibility study How conducive is the context (sector, components, project regions) with regard to the projects’ objective? How feasible is achieving the proposed project outcome and the underlying Theory of Change as well as the proposed indicators? And how coherent is the proposed intervention across sectors, outputs and countries? Which critical assumptions underpin the project's Theory of Change, and to what extent are these assumptions supported by available evidence and stakeholder perspectives? Which factors are most likely to influence whether increased enrolment and attendance translate into improved learning outcomes for children with disabilities? How can the study findings contribute to adaptive management, organisational learning and project refinement across all three countries? 2. Methodology What participatory methods, tools, and resources will be used for data collection and analysis (incl. recommendation of baseline and endline tools)? Which stakeholders will be involved? What are their backgrounds and interests? How can meaningful participation of children with disabilities, caregivers, schools, civil society organisations, OPDs and government stakeholders be ensured? 3. Initial situation and problem analysis, on macro- meso- and micro-levels What current problems of children with disabilities have been identified at micro, meso and macro levels, relevant to the proposed project? Which of the causes of these problems will be prioritised and addressed in the project? What existing root causes, local potential, structures (institutions, networks, umbrella organizations etc.) and social mechanisms can be built on? What gaps have been identified in the system? Which existing identification, referral, assessment and support systems for children with disabilities are functioning effectively and where do significant gaps remain? What specialised teaching and learning materials, assistive devices and support services are currently available, and where are the most significant gaps? To what extent can existing education assessment systems be adapted to different impairment groups, and what constraints currently limit equitable assessment of learning outcomes? What currently prevents children with disabilities from progressing from enrolment to meaningful participation and improvements in foundational literacy and numeracy? Are there any approaches or results from previous development measures? If yes, how can they be extended? Which existing government, community and OPD structures should be strengthened rather than duplicated by the project? What other circumstances, for example conflict dynamics, must be taken into account in the context of the selected countries? 4. Local project partners in the partner countries Which organisations have been selected as local project partners, and why? How will the local project partners’ ownership be improved? Are the partners’ resources and strengths, both individually and at an organisational level, well understood? To what extent does the project planning align with the current capacities of the local partners Tesfa Birhan, Saama Kairo Federation, Chibombo/Mumbwa Child Development Agency, Kafue Child Development Agency? Is selective support from staff of the ChildFund International Country Offices necessary and justified and which project functions can realistically be led by the local partners themselves? What coordination structure between the local partners is recommended? What relevant technical, methodological and advocacy competencies will be further developed within the local partners through the project to strengthen their long-term capacity for implementation, coordination and advocacy? 5. Beneficiaries and other stakeholders (on a micro-, meso- and macro-level) How (with which criteria) will the direct beneficiaries be selected, and by whom? Which groups of children with disabilities are most likely to benefit from the proposed intervention as currently designed, and which groups may require adapted approaches or additional support measures? How is the diversity within the target groups, including disability type, age, gender, socio-economic situation and location, and to what extent must the project take this into account? How can different disability groups can be meaningfully included and the proposed interventions be adapted to address the specific needs of different impairment groups and support requirements? What potential do the beneficiaries have for self-help? Do the beneficiaries and other stakeholders have a common understanding of the problems, prioritising process and objectives of the project? Do the interests of other stakeholders align? Do any conflicts of interest exist? How strong is the various stakeholders’ support for the project, for example, in terms of their own contribution? In what ways might they influence the project? 6. Multi-Country Dimension What is the added value of implementing the proposed project with a multi-country approach compared to stand-alone country projects? What common objective – beyond progress within each country – justifies the multi-country approach? Does this justify the additional complexity and coordination effort of a three-country programme? What is the rationale for the selection of Ethiopia, The Gambia and Zambia? What are the relationships between the three project countries and what are shared and country-specific barriers, opportunities for cross-country learning and potential for joint advocacy and knowledge exchange? Could a project with only two countries achieve similar results more effectively? What existing (cross-national) structures does the project build upon, and what will remain after the project ends? How can sustainability be ensured across all three countries, and into which umbrella organization, active in all three countries, can results of the project be incorporated; and what lasting mechanisms for cooperation, joint learning and advocacy could be established or strengthened? 7. Strategic and Financial Feasibility How realistic is the proposed intervention design under the available budget envelope? Are any adjustments required to the indicators, baseline and target values to ensure they are achievable, measurable and aligned with the proposed intervention design and budget? What are potential simplifications and prioritization options, and which project components are essential to preserve the intended outcomes and Theory of Change? Which elements of the proposed intervention are most likely to be institutionalised and financed by local actors after project completion, and what mechanisms or arrangements are required to sustain both project results and cross-country cooperation beyond external funding? Study Methodology The study will comprise both desk-based research and fieldwork. It will involve a combination of primary data collection and secondary data review. Selected secondary data sources will be made available to the contractor. The following documents will be provided: Initial concept note for the planned project Draft impact matrix Draft theory of change Initial problem analysis conducted by the partners Partner documents relevant to the planned project Selected national strategy documents, background papers, references For the collection of primary data, the contractor is encouraged to propose appropriate methodological approaches (quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods). The study methodology should, where appropriate and ethically feasible, include the direct participation of the project’s primary target group – children with disabilities. The study should ensure that the voices and perspectives of children with disabilities and their families are reflected in the findings, particularly with regard to their participation in project activities and perceived changes in their living conditions. The contractor is expected to propose appropriate, age-sensitive, and ethically sound data collection methods for engaging with children and youths, in line with relevant safeguarding and ethical standards. In addition, the study should include the following data collection methodologies: Desk and literature review Stakeholder consultations Field visits Key Informant Interviews with partner staff, community leaders, and other relevant stakeholders Focus Group Discussions with intended target groups Household or individual surveys (quantitative data collection) Workshop/validation meeting to review preliminary findings with partners and stakeholders Ethical Consideration It is essential to ensure that the risks of potential harm to participants arising from the data collection process are minimized and clearly outweighed by the potential benefits of the study’s outcomes. The contractor must address critical ethical issues in the design and implementation of the study, ensuring that the rights, safety, and confidentiality of all information providers are fully protected. Key considerations include, but are not limited to: Compliance with legal and regulatory requirements, including permissions for data collection, storage, export, and, where applicable, interviewing or collecting information about children and youth. For Zambia: Research ethics clearance from the Research Ethics Committee, and authorisation from the National Health Research Authority (NHRA) where health-related data (e.g., functional screening) are collected; written authority from the Ministry of Education and the respective DEBS offices to conduct research in schools; and compliance with the Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021 and the Children’s Code Act of 2022. For The Gambia : IRB approval from the university of the Gambia (UTG), Compliance with national child protection and safeguarding regulations, relevant data protection requirements, approvals from MoBSE and Regional Education Directorates, and adherence to ChildFund safeguarding standards when engaging children with disabilities and their caregivers. For Ethiopa : Determine whether ethics review is required, secure federal/regional/woreda and school permissions, and comply with Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024, including special protections for children, disability/health data, storage and cross-border transfer Measures to ensure the secure storage and management of collected data. Protocols to maintain anonymity and confidentiality of participants. Ensuring that participation is voluntary and based on informed consent. Safeguarding the rights and welfare of participants and the communities involved. The contractor should take all reasonable steps to ensure that the study is designed and conducted to: Respect and protect the rights, dignity, and welfare of all participants. Produce technically accurate, reliable, and valid findings. Conduct the study in a transparent, impartial, and accountable manner. Contribute to organizational learning and accountability. Ethical considerations must be an integral part of the study process at all stages to maintain the highest standards of professional conduct. Time Schedule and Deliverables The study will be carried out according to the following timeline and corresponding tasks: Timeline Tasks 1st week of December 2026- Briefing and preparation 2nd week of December- Desk review and preparation of the inception report 2nd week of December- Review of inception report by the project team 3rd week of December - Finalization of the inception report 3rd and 4th week of December- Development of data collection tools 1st week of January- Primary data collection and Field visit(s) 2nd week of January-Data analysis 3rd week of January-Drafting of the preliminary study report and Presentation of preliminary findings / validation workshop 4th week of January-Review of draft preliminary study report by the project team End of January 2027-Finalization of the study report and final submission Each deliverable is expected to be submitted according to the agreed timeline, ensuring sufficient time for review and feedback from the project team. Deliverables Inception Report: The contractor should prepare an inception report before commencing the full data collection exercise. The report should detail the contractor’s understanding of the planned project and the study, explaining how each question will be addressed through proposed methods, data sources, and data collection procedures. It should also include a proposed schedule of tasks, activities, and deliverables. Preliminary Study Report: The contractor should provide a concise report presenting all preliminary findings, conclusions, and recommendations. The methodology used should also be described. Expertise Profile of the Study Team The study will be conducted by a lead consultant with proven experience in conducting feasibility studies for development projects and sectorial expertise in inclusive education, supported by qualified local consultants in the three countries. title: Regional Safety & Security Director
description:
The International Rescue Committee (IRC) responds to the world's worst humanitarian crises, helping to restore health, safety, education, economic wellbeing, and power to people devastated by conflict and disaster. Founded in 1933 at the call of Albert Einstein, the IRC is one of the world's largest international humanitarian non-governmental organizations (INGO), at work in more than 40 countries and 29 U.S. cities helping people to survive, reclaim control of their future and strengthen their communities. A force for humanity, IRC employees deliver lasting impact by restoring safety, dignity and hope to millions. If you're a solutions-driven, passionate change-maker, come join us in positively impacting the lives of millions of people world-wide for a better future. Context The East Africa region supports effective, efficient, and high-quality programming by strengthening capacity around client outcomes, program quality, strategic positioning, and business development. It addresses overlapping humanitarian and development challenges – conflict, weak governance, and environmental degradation – through integrated, impactful approaches. The region prioritizes cross-learning, innovation, and harmonized technical strategies, especially in high-need areas. It ensures continuity of care and coordinated service delivery for clients on the move, while advancing strategic donor engagement through cohesive fundraising and regional collaboration. The region responds swiftly to country program needs, filling critical gaps and navigating access constraints, emergencies, and security shifts. It amplifies client and frontline voices to inform global advocacy and fosters strong team cohesion to enhance program delivery. EA focuses on cost-efficient and adaptive approaches to the evolving humanitarian and donor landscape, with a clear focus on resourcing country programs. The EA region operates country programs in Uganda, Kenya, Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, and Ethiopia. Position Summary The Regional Safety and Security Director (RSSD) is one of the most senior leadership roles in the East Africa region and provides strategic leadership for safety, security, and humanitarian access across the region. They set and drive the implementation of a comprehensive strategy to anticipate, analyze, and mitigate risks, safeguard staff and assets, enable principled humanitarian access, and ensure the continuity of IRC’s operations and programs in complex and high-risk environments. As the principal safety and security advisor to, and close partner of, the Regional Vice President (RVP), the RSSD works alongside the RVP on the decisions that shape IRC’s presence, access, and continuity across the region. They are a full member of the Regional Management Team and of IRC’s global safety and security (S&S) team. Within the Regional Management Team, the RSSD contributes as a senior leader to regional strategy, priorities, and decision-making, not only as the safety and security function, bringing a risk-informed perspective to program, operational, and resourcing choices. They integrate Gender, Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (GEDI) informed security risk analysis into strategic, operational, programmatic, and partnership decisions so that security considerations are embedded across IRC’s work. Reporting jointly to the RVP and the Senior Director for Safety and Security (SDSS), the RSSD operates with significant autonomy and influence. Working in close partnership with Country Directors, they ensure that each country program has robust, context-appropriate protocols, systems, and capacities in place to address unique threats and challenges, while remaining agile to adapt to shifting environments. The RSSD maintains in-depth knowledge of security dynamics across all EA countries, monitors early warning indicators, and deploys regularly, including at short notice, to support local teams. They play a central role in mentoring and building the capabilities of IRC staff and leaders to operate safely and effectively, thereby strengthening IRC’s ability to reach and serve the most affected and underserved populations. Responsibilities Strategic Leadership and Regional Management As a member of the Regional Management Team, contribute as a senior leader to regional strategy, priority-setting, and decision-making, bringing a risk-informed perspective to program, operational, and resourcing choices across the region rather than representing the safety and security function alone. Serve as the principal safety and security advisor to, and close partner of, the RVP, enabling timely, risk-informed decisions on humanitarian access, operational continuity, and duty of care, and jointly activating and leading crisis management when required. Partner with Country Directors to align safety, security, and humanitarian access with country Strategy Action Plans (SAPs) and operational priorities, supporting their decision-making and accountability for risk. Security Risk Management Lead and supervise the identification, analysis, and mitigation of S&S risks across the region, ensuring alignment with IRC’s global standards. Guide and support Country Directors and field leaders to adapt and implement context-specific security risk management strategies ensuring proactive risk identification, mitigation, and emergency preparedness. Review, monitor, and encourage compliance with the Security Minimum Standards (SMS) in all country programs providing follow-up and technical guidance where gaps are identified. Drive and champion the development, adaptation, and roll-out of global and regional initiatives on duty of care and safeguarding, embedding these into operational culture and practice. Shape and strengthen safety and security policies, procedures, and practices that fully integrate Gender Equality, Diversity, and Inclusion (GEDI) principles as well as Partnership Excellence for Equality and Results System (PEERS) commitments. Extend IRC’s security capacity to partners, ensuring they receive tailored risk management support, access to systems, and benefit from IRC’s standards relevant to their operational contexts. Build and maintain an active network of IRC security focal points across country programs and cultivate strong external relationships with professional contacts, peer agencies, and security counterparts to enhance collective risk management. Humanitarian Access Management Enable and safeguard principled, secure, and sustained humanitarian access across country programs, ensuring communities can be reached and served in line with IRC’s country Strategy Action Plans (SAP). Strengthen and expand humanitarian access teams and capabilities across the region, building skills, systems, and approaches that enhance operational reach and acceptance. Develop, adapt, and implement context-specific guidelines for humanitarian access and engagement with state and non-state actors, ensuring alignment with IRC policy, international humanitarian law, and standards. Advise and guide country programs in the design of operational and programmatic contingency plans ensuring preparedness for sudden shifts in political, security, or conflict dynamics. Collaborate with relevant IRC units to ensure prompt and appropriate follow-up to violations of IRC’s Code of Conduct and breaches of humanitarian principles, reinforcing accountability and ethical operations. Performance Management and Development Lead and actively contribute to the recruitment and selection of key positions with S&S responsibilities, ensuring high-caliber talent and diverse representation. Co-manage and mentor direct-report staff (under the Management in Partnership (MiP) model with Country Directors), setting clear expectations, defining performance objectives, providing regular, timely feedback, and conducting documented performance reviews that drive accountability and growth. Promote and safeguard staff well-being, monitoring staff care across the region and supporting appropriate interventions to address the needs of both national and international staff. Directly supervise and develop the Regional Humanitarian Access and Safety Coordinator, ensuring progressive and forward-looking S&S plans that align with regional priorities and organizational strategy. Learning & Development Design, support, and supervise the implementation of regional capacity-building plans, ensuring effective delivery of IRC’s global S&S training programs across EA country programs. Embed gender-sensitive approaches into all capacity development and learning initiatives, addressing gender-specific risks and ensuring inclusivity in staff preparedness. Lead and facilitate critical incident management trainings and simulations, in close coordination with the global S&S unit to strengthen preparedness and response capacities across the region. Incident Management Support country programs to ensure timely, accurate, and high-quality incident notification, reporting, analysis, and dissemination of lessons learned. Serve as a member of the Regional Incident Management Team actively supporting the RVP in the management and resolution of Tier 2 and Tier 3 incidents. Facilitate After-Action Reviews ensuring that corrective measures are clearly defined, documented, and systematically implemented in line with established incident protocols. Oversee and monitor the SHIELD incident database producing quarterly trend analyses to inform strategic decision-making and strengthen regional risk mitigation. Key Working Relationships Reports to: Regional Vice President, East Africa, and Senior Director, Global Safety & Security (matrixed reporting) Member of: Regional Management Team and IRC’s global Safety & Security team Partners closely with: the Regional Vice President, as principal safety and security advisor, and Country Directors on country risk, humanitarian access, and duty of care Manages: Regional Humanitarian Access & Security Coordinator; and, through Management in Partnership with the respective Country Directors, country Security Leads Collaborates with: fellow Regional Safety & Security Directors, the Director of Security Learning & Operations, the Global Duty of Care Director, People & Culture, and other members of the Regional Management Team; and, externally, with peer agencies, security networks, and relevant counterparts Qualifications & Requirements At least 10 years’ experience in international humanitarian assistance, with proven ability to plan, organize, and lead security management operations. Prior experience in EA with strong knowledge of regional and country dynamics is essential. Fluency in English required; proficiency in a relevant regional language (e.g. Arabic, Amharic, Somali, or Swahili) is an asset. Demonstrated grounding in humanitarian principles, codes of conduct, NGO culture, and proven success in gender-sensitive security management and gender equality. Skilled at influencing without authority and building effective relationships across multinational teams, partners, and stakeholders. Demonstrated ability to transfer knowledge through mentoring, coaching, and non-formal methods. Strong capacity to analyze and present complex security dynamics and incidents clearly and on short notice, highlighting implications for operations. Willingness and ability to travel up to 40% of the time. Work Environment This position is open to both national and international applicants, in the locations indicated as well as potentially other IRC locations open to hosting. We will, however, prioritize consideration of national candidates from the region and for which our highly competitive national salary scale and benefits will apply. Returning National Candidates: We strongly encourage national or returning national candidates to apply for this position. If you are a citizen of the Country in which this position is based, are currently located outside your home country, and possess over 4 years of international work experience, the IRC has introduced an attractive remuneration package. The package includes competitive compensation, return flight to post, shipping allowance, temporary housing, and a relocation allowance. Certain restrictions may apply. IRC strives to attract, motivate, and retain qualified national staff in our programs. Gender Equality, Diversity and Inclusion: at IRC, we are passionate about creating an inclusive workplace that promotes and values diversity. Organizations that are diverse in age, gender identity, race, sexual orientation, physical or mental ability, ethnicity, nationality, and perspective are validated to be better organizations. More importantly, creating a safe workspace environment where everyone, from any background, can do their best is the right thing to do. So, bring your whole self to work. We particularly encourage qualified women to apply for this role, and are committed to supporting them through flexible working arrangements, safety and duty of care planning tailored to the East African countries’ context, and a workplace culture that values the leadership women bring to humanitarian response. In keeping with our core values of Integrity, Service, Accountability and Equality, IRC strives to maintain a work environment built on mutual respect in which all individuals treat each other professionally, and free of bias, prejudice, and harassment. IRC expressly prohibits and will not tolerate discrimination, harassment, retaliation, or bullying of IRC Persons in any work setting. All IRC staff, wherever they are located, are accountable for creating an environment free of discrimination, harassment, bullying, and retaliation. Professional Standards: All International Rescue Committee workers must adhere to the core values and principles outlined in IRC Way - Standards for Professional Conduct . Our Standards are Integrity, Service, Equality and Accountability. In accordance with these values, the IRC operates and enforces policies on Safeguarding , Conflicts of Interest, Fiscal Integrity, and Reporting Wrongdoing and Protection from Retaliation. IRC is committed to take all necessary preventive measures and create an environment where people feel safe, and to take all necessary actions and corrective measures when harm occurs. IRC builds teams of professionals who promote critical reflection, power sharing, debate, and objectivity to deliver the best possible services to our clients.

title: ETHIOPIA - FIELD COORDINATOR (M/F) - TIGRAY
description:
Desired start date: 01/12/2026 Duration of the mission: 6 Months Location: Adwa - Tigray Region SOLIDARITES INTERNATIONAL (SI) is an international humanitarian aid association which, since more than 40 years, has been providing assistance to populations affected by armed conflicts and natural disasters by meeting their basic needs for food, water and shelter. Particularly committed to the fight against diseases linked to unsafe water, the leading cause of death in the world, SI's interventions provide expertise in the field of access to drinking water, sanitation and hygiene promotion, but also in the essential area of food security and livelihoods. Present in 26 countries, the SI teams – 3200 people in total, made up of expatriates, national staff, permanent staff at HQ, and a few volunteers - intervene with professionalism and commitment while respecting cultural norms. PRESENTATION OF THE MISSION: Solidarités International (SI) was registered in Ethiopia in December 2022, having previously implemented a WASH in Health intervention in Jijiga, Somali Region, in 2017. In November 2023, SI became the first humanitarian actor to operate in Mao Komo Special woreda (Benishangul-Gumuz) by rehabilitating water points in areas that had been inaccessible for three years. Currently, SI is operational in two regions of the country (In Tigray Region and Amhara Region). In Tigray, bordering Eritrea, focusing on hard-to-reach areas in partnership with Mums for Mums (MfM) SI is implementing an emergency multisectoral humanitarian programme in Ahsea and Rama Woredas of central zone, to support communities affected by drought, conflict, and displacement. Running from September 2024 to December 2025 (which is now to be extended until end of June 2026), the project aims to improve access to safe water, health services, and nutrition support, while addressing gender-based violence and mental health needs. Key activities include rehabilitating water systems and health facilities, community-based malnutrition screening, cash assistance for vulnerable households, and capacity-building for local actors. In Amhara region, Solidarités International (SI) and Première Urgence Internationale (PUI) are jointly implementing an integrated emergency response program in the Amhara region of Ethiopia, primarily focused on Health and Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) services. This program is part of a wider effort to address the significant humanitarian needs in the region caused by ongoing conflict and displacement. SI has been granted cost extension (the donor contract is extended until end of June 2026 with additional fund allocation) of existing project in Tigray and is looking for a Field Coordinator to continue the project activities in the same area. GENERAL OBJECTIVES : The Field Coordinator is the representative of the organization at field level. He/she proposes a strategy for his/her area, according to the geopolitical and humanitarian context, and ensures its implementation once validated. He/she checks and ensures that projects are carried out in accordance with the Solidarités International charter, respecting all internal and contractual procedures. He/she mobilizes the material and financial resources necessary for programs to run smoothly and supervises resource management. He/she coordinates the teams in place and is responsible for their security in his/her assigned zone. Representation and Internal / external communication: The FC is the official representative of Solidarités International in his/her intervention zone for NGOs, administrative, political and local authorities and civil society. Maintain adequate preparedness for a potential deterioration of the security situation, including possible disruption of banking services, communications and movements. Main operational constraints include possible access restrictions, interruptions to telecommunications and internet, fuel shortages, banking/cash limitations and disruptions to road movements. Some operational areas may have limited or no network coverage, requiring reinforced movement tracking and communication procedures. LANGUAGES : Fluency in written and spoken English is essential. Knowledge of the local language(s) (e.g., Amharic, Tigrigna) is a strong asset. SI WILL OFFER YOU : A salaried position: According to experience, starting from EUR 3080 gross per month (2800 base salary + 10% annual leave allowance paid monthly) and a monthly Per Diem of USD 400.
